page_title: Moving from orchestration to choregraphy - Part 1

sources.entry: Moving from orchestration to choreography - By Olivier Jauze, March 2021. Michelin's journey from BPM orchestration to event-driven choreography. It's the first of a series and continues with part 2 and part 3.

summary.title: Moving from orchestration to choregraphy - Part 1
summary.one_liner: Michelin's account of replacing a central BPM orchestrator that ran its tire-distribution processes with an event-driven choreography of microservices, and the organizational arguments that won the decision.
keywords: choreography vs orchestration pros and cons
how to replace a workflow engine
takeaways: Michelin decomposed a mainframe monolith into COTS systems (DRP, TMS, WMS) coordinated by a central BPM orchestrator, which later became a single point of failure and a maintenance burden.
Choreography replaces a central orchestrator with services that subscribe to and publish business events, improving modularity and making it easier to add steps.
Losing the orchestrator also loses built-in end-to-end monitoring, so the approach requires every component to publish events and separate business monitoring tools.
Organizational concerns (central control, maintainability, team ownership) shaped the design; Michelin kept a central team as a compromise.
A proof of concept covering redevelopment effort, scalability/availability and monitoring secured the decision; the stack is covered in Part 2.
summary.summary: The article is Part 1 of a three-part series by Michelin engineers on moving a tire logistics platform from a BPM orchestrator to an event-driven choreography of microservices. It explains the history: a mainframe monolith decomposed into COTS systems, then a central BPM orchestrator carrying about 17 BPMN processes, and the problems that followed (single point of failure, aging BPM engines, logic pushed into the orchestrator, and loss of in-house knowledge). It then discusses the trade-offs between orchestration and choreography, drawing on Bernd Rücker's views, and addresses concerns about monitoring, centralized intelligence and maintainability. The page ends by noting a proof of concept led to the decision, with the technology stack deferred to Part 2.
